```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  dpi = 110,
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

```{r libs, message = FALSE}
library(brouillet)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The problem

Here is a field where the signal worth seeing sits in a narrow band around
zero, and the extremes are saturated regions you already know about.

```{r data}
set.seed(42)

grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 80), y = seq(0, 1, length.out = 80))
grid$z <- with(grid, 2.4 * sin(2.1 * pi * x) * cos(1.6 * pi * y) +
                 0.6 * sin(3.3 * pi * (x + y)))

show_map <- function(params, title, limits = c(-2, 2)) {
  ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, fill = z)) +
    geom_raster() +
    asScaleFillGradient(params, limits = limits, na.value = "grey90") +
    coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "z") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
          legend.key.width = unit(8, "pt"))
}
```

A plain linear ramp spends most of its range on pale pinks and blues:

```{r linear}
DIV <- c("navy", "white", "firebrick")

plain <- gradientParams(DIV, midpoints = 0.5, gradient_mode = "linear")
show_map(plain, "linear ramp")
```

## A specification is an object

Everything in brouillet starts with a specification. It describes a gradient
and nothing about your data, so the same object works on any range.

```{r spec}
p <- gradientParams(DIV, midpoints = 0.5, width = 0.25)
p
```

Two coordinates are in play, and they are not the same thing:

- `midpoints` places the **colour stops**, as fractions of the range. Here
  `white` sits halfway between `navy` and `firebrick`.
- `center`, `width` and `asymmetry` shape the **curve inside each segment**:
  how fast the colour changes as you move through it.

## Controlling the curve

`width` is the span over which the curve goes from 5% to 95%. Narrowing it
compresses the middle of the range and expands the extremes, which is the
colour equivalent of turning up contrast.

```{r width}
show_map(gradientParams(DIV, midpoints = 0.5, width = 0.25), "width = 0.25")
```

The parameters mean what they say, which you can check directly:

```{r curve-measure}
x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 20001)
y <- contrastCurve(x, center = 0.5, width = 0.25)

x[which(y >= 0.5)[1]]
x[which(y >= 0.95)[1]] - x[which(y >= 0.05)[1]]
```

`center` moves the transition along the range. Push it up and only strongly
positive values turn red:

```{r center}
show_map(gradientParams(DIV, midpoints = 0.5, width = 0.25, center = 0.72),
         "center = 0.72")
```

`asymmetry` decides which side rolls off slowly. Positive values are sharp
below `center` and gradual above it:

```{r asymmetry, fig.height = 2.6}
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(-0.8, 0, 0.8), function(a) {
  data.frame(x = x, y = contrastCurve(x, width = 0.4, asymmetry = a),
             asymmetry = factor(a))
}))

ggplot(curves, aes(x, y, colour = asymmetry)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "position in data", y = "position in ramp") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

Setting `gradient_mode = "linear"` uses the same vocabulary with straight lines
instead of logistics: `width = 1` is an ordinary ramp, and `width < 1` leaves
flat regions at both ends.

## Out-of-range colours

Give values beyond the limits their own colours, and they appear as bands on
the colourbar rather than vanishing into `na.value`.

```{r clip}
clipped <- gradientParams(DIV, midpoints = 0.5, width = 0.3,
                          low.clip.color = "grey35",
                          high.clip.color = "gold")

show_map(clipped, "clipped beyond +/- 2")
```

```{r clip-values}
asColorFun(clipped, limits = c(-2, 2))(c(-99, -2, 0, 2, 99, NA))
```

Setting only one side is fine: the other end keeps the gradient's own colour.
`blend.clip = TRUE` fades the clip colour in rather than switching abruptly.

One trap worth stating plainly: if your code squishes values into range before
plotting, nothing is ever out of range and the clip colours can never fire.

```{r squish}
raw <- c(-0.4, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.4)
f <- asColorFun(gradientParams(c("white", "red"), low.clip.color = "grey30",
                               high.clip.color = "gold"))

f(raw)
f(scales::oob_squish_any(raw, range = c(0, 1)))
```

## One specification, several outputs

The same object becomes whatever the plotting system needs.

```{r outputs}
col_fun <- asColorFun(p, limits = c(-2, 2))
col_fun(c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2))

head(buildGradient(p, limits = c(-2, 2)), 3)

class(asScaleFillGradient(p, limits = c(-2, 2)))
```

`asColorFun()` is interface-compatible with `circlize::colorRamp2()`, so a
specification also drives `ComplexHeatmap`, base graphics and raster export,
not only ggplot2. `previewGradient(p)` renders one as a bar when you just want
to look at it.

## Templates: one shape, many palettes

When the curve and clipping are a house style but the colours vary per figure,
describe the shape once and supply colours later.

```{r template}
house <- gradientTemplate(width = 0.25, high.clip.color = "gold")
house

withColors(house, c("black", "orange"))
```

`updateGradient()` edits an existing specification and revalidates the result,
which is the right way to tweak one you were handed:

```{r update}
updateGradient(p, width = 0.1)$width
updateGradient(p, high.clip.color = NULL)$high.clip.color
```

## Multi-stop gradients

Any number of colours, with `length(colors) - 2` interior stops.

```{r multi}
multi <- gradientParams(c("black", "navy", "white", "firebrick", "gold"),
                        midpoints = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.75), width = 0.3)

asColorFun(multi, limits = c(-2, 2))(c(-2, -1.2, 0, 1, 2))
show_map(multi, "five stops")
```

The curve applies **within each segment**, not across the whole ramp, so with
many stops a narrow `width` sharpens every transition and posterises the result.
That is sometimes what you want; if it is not, use two or three colours.

## Curves you define yourself

Any vectorised, non-decreasing function from `[0, 1]` to `[0, 1]` can drive the
mapping. The most useful case is histogram equalisation, where every quantile of
the data gets an equal share of the colour range.

```{r custom}
skewed <- rlnorm(4000)
lims <- c(0, unname(quantile(skewed, 0.99)))

equalise <- function(values, limits) {
  f <- stats::ecdf(values)
  lo <- f(limits[1]); hi <- f(limits[2])
  function(x) {
    y <- f(limits[1] + x * (limits[2] - limits[1]))
    if (hi > lo) (y - lo) / (hi - lo) else y
  }
}

eq <- gradientParams(c("white", "navy"), gradient_mode = "custom",
                     mapping_fun = equalise(skewed, lims))

asColorFun(eq, limits = lims)(quantile(skewed, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)))
```

The requirements are checked when the specification is built, not at plot time,
so a bad mapping fails at the call site.

## Using brouillet inside your own function

Accept a specification, and fall back to a default when none is given:

```{r integration, eval = FALSE}
myPlot <- function(data, fill.gradient = NULL, limits = range(data$z)) {

  if (is.null(fill.gradient)) {
    fill.gradient <- brouillet::gradientParams(c("white", "firebrick"))
  }
  if (inherits(fill.gradient, "brouillet_gradient_template")) {
    fill.gradient <- brouillet::withColors(fill.gradient, c("white", "firebrick"))
  }

  ggplot(data, aes(x, y, fill = z)) +
    geom_raster() +
    brouillet::asScaleFillGradient(fill.gradient, limits = limits)
}
```

Accepting templates as well as full specifications lets callers change the
curve without restating your palette.

If your function already exposes `low`/`mid`/`high` colour arguments and a
midpoint in data units, convert the midpoint with `relativeMidpoint()`:

```{r relmid}
relativeMidpoint(0, c(-2, 2))
```

It errors on `NA` and on values outside the limits, and warns when a midpoint
sits exactly on a limit, because such a midpoint cannot be an interior stop.
Screen for those cases and fall back to a two-colour ramp.

## Where this sits

`ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn()` already interpolates supplied stops in CIE
Lab, and brouillet delegates to the same function, so colours match exactly.
For designing a palette in the first place, `colorspace` is the better tool.
What brouillet adds is the contrast curve, two-sided clipping visible on the
colourbar, and one specification object that converts to every output form.

See `?gradientParams` and the README for the full reference.
